newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Ultramar CEO says bigger is better.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ultramar CEO says bigger is better.

text.p: Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Corp, which Tuesday said it will buy Total SA's North American unit for $811 million, is likely to be hunting for more refining assets after it digests its latest acquisition, the company's top executive said.

"After we swallow this acquistion, maybe we'll be more aggressive. But for now we have to focus on the integration," Ultramar Diamond Chief Executive Roger Hemminghaus told Reuters in a telephone interview Wednesday.
But bigger is better, says Hemminghaus, and he plans for Ultramar to be a survivor in what he sees as the continuing shakeout in U.S. downstream oil sector.
"I see the industry continuing to go through consolidation. We'll continue obviously to look for possibilities to expand our throughput," Hemminghaus said.

He said Ultramar would focus its acquisition efforts in areas where it already has a strategic presence. The Total deal includes three small refineries and retail assets in Colorado, Oklahoma and Michigan, and dovetails with Ultramar's operating areas in the U.S. Southwest and eastern Canada.
"We've told people that if there are pieces that fall out of (other) joint venture and consolidations, and if they're in our marketing sphere, then maybe we'd be interested," he said.

Among the wave of mergers and takeovers in the past year was the largest in the industry's history -- Shell Oil and Texaco are merging their $10 billion of U.S. refining assets in a deal which is expected to include the Texaco/Saudi Aramco joint venture, Star Enterprises.

Also, Tosco Corp bought assets from BP America, Unocal sold California and MidWest downstream assets to Tosco and Petroleos de Venezuela, respectivley, and Valero Energy Corp bought Salomon Brothers refineries.

After its latest buy, Hemminghaus's company -- itself a result of last year's Ultramar merger with Diamond Shamrock -- ends up with about 650,000 barrels per day throughput, ranking about eighth largest refiner in the U.S.

Pressed on whether the three Total refineries lack the critical mass to be money makers in the fiercely competitive U.S. refining sector, Hemminghaus said the Denver, Colo., and Alma, Mich., plants are in niche markets that obviate many competitive concerns that exist in busier markets.
He also noted that Total has spent $250 million in the last five years at the Ardmore, Okla., refinery aimed at running cheaper West Texas Sour crudes that will cut operating costs.
"That's a significant advantage to run lower-cost crudes in that part of the country," Hemminghaus said, noting the Oklahoma plant can now run 70 percent WTS.
He also said Ultramar plans to expand the Ardmore refinery over the next two years so that it can handle about 85,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude, up from 68,000 bpd currently.
"I think we can add significant value by increasing throughput and running the cheaper crude," he said.
"This deal is a key step of the strategy of improving our overall competitive position and reducing our cost-per-barrel structure," the Ultramar chief said.
The merged company will have seven refineries, 6,381 branded outlets in 19 states and six Canadian provinces, and over 23,000 employees.
Hemminghaus reckons job cuts will total about 200, mainly non-union white collar workers in corporate and administrative positions.
